title: UK Inflation Hits 3.6%: What It Means for Savers and Tracker Borrowers
summary: UK CPI rose to 3.6% in October, a one-year high, with Bank Rate at 4% after the first hike since 2023. On our figures a 4% savings rate now earns about 0.4% after inflation, and a tracker borrower with GBP 200,000 owes about GBP 29 a month more after the hike.
description:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in the year to October 2026, from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. It is the highest rate in a year and the fourth monthly rise in a row, up from a low of 2.6% in June. Prices rose 0.5% in the month. Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.8%, and services inflation held at 3.7%, slightly below the 3.8% economists had expected.

The rise was driven mainly by motor fuels, with diesel at a record price, and by tobacco tax increases that took effect earlier than last year. Food inflation slowed to 0.9%, its lowest in more than five years. The CPIH measure, which includes owner occupiers' housing costs, rose to 3.7%.

The figure came in just below the Bank of England's own forecast of 3.7%. On November 5 the Bank raised Bank Rate by a quarter point to 4%, its first increase since August 2023, and it expects inflation to approach 5% by the middle of 2027 as higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict feed through. Markets trimmed the chance of another rise in December to about 80% after the data, but still price three or four quarter-point increases by the end of 2027.

This PolicyRix Team analysis turns those numbers into what they mean for savings and mortgage payments.

Savers: the real return is thin

The real return on savings is what is left after inflation. Using the standard formula, (1 + interest rate) divided by (1 + inflation) minus 1, a savings account paying 4% gives a real return of about 0.4% at 3.6% inflation. An account paying 3.5% loses about 0.1% a year in real terms. One paying 4.5% gives about 0.9%. These rates are illustrations; actual rates vary widely, and many easy-access accounts pay less than Bank Rate.

On GBP 10,000, the difference between a 3.5% account and a 4.5% account is GBP 100 a year before tax. Interest above the Personal Savings Allowance, GBP 1,000 for basic-rate and GBP 500 for higher-rate taxpayers, is taxed, which pushes real returns lower for larger balances outside an ISA. If inflation rises towards the Bank's 5% projection and savings rates do not follow, real returns on many accounts would turn negative.

Tracker borrowers: the hike in pounds

Tracker mortgages move with Bank Rate. Take a GBP 200,000 repayment mortgage over 25 years at Bank Rate plus 0.75 percentage points. Before the November hike, the rate was 4.5% and the monthly payment about GBP 1,112. After the hike, at 4.75%, it is about GBP 1,140, an increase of about GBP 29 a month, or about GBP 343 a year.

If Bank Rate rises by another three quarter-points to 4.75%, as markets broadly expect by the end of 2027, the same tracker would be at 5.5% and cost about GBP 1,228 a month, about GBP 117 more than before November. Four rises would take it to 5.75% and about GBP 1,258. These figures are our own calculations using a standard repayment formula.

Fixed-rate borrowers are protected until their deal ends, but new fixed rates are priced off market expectations, which already include future rises. Anyone whose fixed deal ends in 2027 should look at their likely new payment now and consider securing a deal up to six months early, which many lenders allow.

Energy bills come next

Governor Andrew Bailey has said a recent fall in wholesale energy prices came too late to offset a roughly 20% rise in regulated household energy bills due in January. That increase will feed into inflation early next year and is the main reason the Bank expects inflation to keep rising. Households can check whether a fixed energy tariff is available below the new cap before January.

What the data cannot tell us

One month's figure says little about the path ahead; the Bank's forecast depends heavily on energy prices and the conflict. Our savings examples ignore tax, and our tracker example uses a single margin; real tracker margins vary by lender and loan-to-value. Market pricing of future rate rises changes daily and is not a forecast of what the Bank will do. And headline inflation is an average: households that drive a lot or use more energy face a higher personal rate than 3.6%, while those spending more on food may face a lower one.

The short version: inflation is edging up, savings are barely beating it, and tracker borrowers are paying more, with the Bank signalling that this may not be the last rise.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of ONS CPI data for October 2026 and Bank of England Monetary Policy Report (November 2026), with reporting from RTE/Reuters, The Intermediary and Trading Economics
key_points: UK CPI rose to 3.6% in October from 3.5%, a one-year high; core held at 2.8% and services at 3.7%.
Fuel and earlier tobacco tax rises drove the increase, while food inflation slowed to 0.9%.
Bank Rate is 4% after the first hike since 2023; markets see about an 80% chance of another rise in December.
On our calculation a 4% savings rate earns about 0.4% after inflation; a 3.5% rate loses about 0.1%.
A GBP 200,000 tracker at Bank Rate plus 0.75 costs about GBP 29 a month more after the hike, and about GBP 117 more if three further rises follow.
why_it_matters: Inflation and Bank Rate decide whether savings keep their value and what millions of tracker and remortgaging borrowers pay. Converting the figures into pounds shows the squeeze is modest now but could grow through 2027.

title: Who Should Refinance at 7.11%? Break-Even by Loan Vintage
summary: Refinance demand is about 60% below a year ago even after four weeks of falling rates. Our break-even analysis shows why: a buyer from the October peak at 7.40% would take about 12 years to recover costs at today's 7.11%, while a 2023 borrower at 7.79% breaks even in under four years.
description:
US mortgage rates have fallen for four straight weeks, but most homeowners still have no reason to refinance. Freddie Mac's 30-year average stood at 7.11% on November 12, down from 7.40% in mid-October. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own measure of contract rates fell to 7.21% in the week ending November 6, and refinance applications rose 4.5% that week, a third straight weekly gain. Yet the MBA's refinance index remains about 60% below its level a year earlier, and refinances made up just under 40% of applications.

The reason is simple arithmetic: refinancing only pays when the new rate is well below the old one. A year ago the average 30-year rate was 6.24%, so the millions who borrowed in 2024 and 2025 already have lower rates than anything on offer today. This PolicyRix Team analysis works out who can benefit now, using our new Mortgage Refinance Break-Even Calculator.

The assumptions

Each example uses a $350,000 balance and closing costs of $10,500, which is 3% of the loan and in the middle of the common 2% to 5% range. The new loan is a 30-year fixed at today's 7.11% unless stated. We count the monthly principal and interest saving, the simple break-even, and the net gain after seven years, which also counts the balance still owed.

Borrowers from late 2023, at 7.79%

Freddie Mac's 30-year average peaked at 7.79% in October 2023. A borrower at that rate with 27 years left pays about $2,590 a month. Refinancing into a 30-year loan at 7.11% cuts that to about $2,354, a saving of about $236. Break-even is about 45 months, just under four years, and the net gain after seven years is about $4,400.

Choosing a 27-year term instead, to avoid adding years, gives a payment of about $2,433, a saving of about $158 and a break-even of about 67 months. But because the debt is not stretched, the seven-year gain rises to about $6,300. This is the trade-off our new guide explains: the simple break-even makes the shorter term look worse when it actually leaves the borrower further ahead.

Buyers from the October 2026 peak, at 7.40%

A buyer who locked 7.40% a month ago pays about $2,423 a month. At 7.11% the new payment is about $2,354, a saving of only about $69. Break-even is about 153 months, nearly 13 years, and after seven years the borrower would be about $3,300 worse off. For this group, refinancing now is a clear loss unless a lender offers a no-cost refinance or a much lower rate.

What a fall to 6.5% would change

Many forecasters do not expect rates to fall quickly, but it helps to know the trigger point. If rates reached 6.5%, the 7.40% buyer would save about $211 a month, break even in about 50 months and be about $11,700 ahead after seven years. The 7.79% borrower would save about $378, break even in about 28 months and be about $19,400 ahead. Borrowers from the recent peak should note that figure and watch for it rather than refinance at today's level.

Ways to improve the numbers

Ask your current lender about a streamlined refinance, which can cut costs. Compare at least three Loan Estimates on the same day. Treat a no-closing-cost offer as a slightly higher rate with zero costs; for people who may move within a few years it can be the better deal. Avoid paying points unless you are confident of staying a long time. And if the main goal is a lower payment, a recast, where the lender re-amortises the loan after a lump-sum payment, can be cheaper than a full refinance.

What the data cannot tell us

Freddie Mac's average is for strong-credit conforming loans; individual offers depend on credit score, equity and loan type, and refinance rates can differ from purchase rates. Our closing costs are an assumption. The examples ignore taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance and any cash-out. The MBA index measures applications, not completed loans. And no one knows where rates will go: the October CPI report and the Federal Reserve's December meeting could move them either way.

The short version: at 7.11%, refinancing makes sense mainly for people who borrowed at 7.75% or more. Everyone else should run their own numbers, note the rate that would make it worthwhile, and wait.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey and MBA Weekly Mortgage Applications Survey data, as reported by Mortgage News Daily, Trading Economics and MPA
key_points: Freddie Mac's 30-year average is 7.11%; the MBA refinance index is still about 60% below a year ago.
A 2023 borrower at 7.79% saves about $236 a month refinancing a $350,000 loan, breaking even in about 45 months.
A buyer from the October 2026 peak at 7.40% saves only about $69 and would need nearly 13 years to break even.
If rates fell to 6.5%, the 7.40% buyer would break even in about 50 months and be about $11,700 ahead after seven years.
A shorter new term lengthens the simple break-even but can leave the borrower further ahead.
why_it_matters: Lenders market every rate dip as a reason to refinance. Running the break-even by loan vintage shows who actually gains now, and the rate that would make waiting borrowers act.

title: Binance's $6.3bn Hack Shows How Little Crypto Theft Is Insured
summary: The $6.3 billion Binance hack is more than four times the previous record, and Binance's own reserve fund covered roughly 16% to 19% of it. We compare the hack with known crypto crime policies and estimate what full hot-wallet cover would cost.
description:
On October 29, hackers drained about $6.3 billion in tokens from Binance's hot wallets, the largest crypto theft on record. According to a report Binance published, the attackers used a fake job interview and malicious software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two Binance engineers, then used a third machine to move the funds. Binance says customers will be made whole from company funds, and it has set aside more than $6.34 billion, including about $5 billion in the affected tokens. Issuers including Tether and Circle froze about $3 billion of the stolen assets.

The attack has turned attention to crypto insurance, and to how little of a loss this size any policy could cover. This PolicyRix Team analysis puts the numbers side by side.

The scale

The previous largest crypto exchange hack hit Bybit in February 2025, at about $1.5 billion. On our arithmetic, the Binance theft is about 4.2 times larger. After withdrawals reopened, customers pulled about $4.72 billion, which Reuters reported as around 3% of platform assets. That implies total platform assets of roughly $157 billion, so the theft itself was about 4% of assets.

What the safety net covered

Binance's Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, set up in 2018 from a share of trading fees, holds crypto assets of roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, according to Binance figures cited by Reuters and others. Against a $6.3 billion loss, that is about 16% to 19%. The rest of the cover is coming from Binance's own corporate balance sheet, not insurance.

Commercial insurance is smaller still. Coinbase has disclosed a crime policy of about $255 million for platform-wide breaches, which would equal about 4% of a loss the size of Binance's. Experts told Reuters that no available crypto insurance could cover a loss of this scale, and many policies exclude state-backed cyberattacks.

What full cover would cost

Specialist estimates put premiums for crime cover on hot-wallet assets, those kept online for trading, at about 3% to 5% of the amount insured each year, against 0.8% to 1.2% for offline cold storage. On those rates, insuring $6.3 billion of hot-wallet assets would cost about $189 million to $315 million a year, if insurers would write it at all. That is why exchanges keep most assets in cold storage, insure a slice, and self-insure the rest through funds like SAFU.

How crypto insurance works

Exchanges typically combine several policies. Crime insurance covers theft and some social engineering, but standard crime policies were built for cash and securities and often exclude crypto unless it is specifically added. Cyber liability covers breach response and regulatory costs, but usually not the value of stolen coins. Specie or digital asset cover protects assets in defined storage, mostly cold wallets. Most of this capacity comes from specialist insurers at Lloyd's and in Bermuda. Common exclusions include price swings, poor key management and fraud by the policyholder.

What changes now

Insurers are not expected to pull back from crypto, but underwriters will ask exchanges and custodians about the specific weaknesses exposed at Binance, including hiring processes and engineer device security, and whether clients hold money with Binance. Gallagher's David Rogers said insurers' first question will be about exposure to Binance itself.

What it means for crypto holders

For individuals, the lesson is that an exchange's insurance is rarely large enough to protect every customer in a major hack. Binance customers are being repaid because the company can afford it, not because insurance pays. Holders should read what an exchange's protection actually covers, keep long-term holdings in self-custody or with regulated custodians that disclose their insurance limits, and spread holdings rather than keep everything on one platform.

What the data cannot tell us

Platform assets and SAFU values move with crypto prices, so our ratios are approximate. Premium ranges come from earlier specialist estimates and may differ today. Binance has not disclosed its commercial insurance, so we cannot say whether any policy will pay. And frozen assets may be recovered, which would reduce the net loss.

The short version: the largest crypto theft ever was covered by the exchange's own money, not by insurance, and the gap between crypto's size and the insurance behind it remains wide.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Business Insurance and Binance disclosures (October and November 2026)
image_alt: Server racks in a data centre (illustrative)
key_points: Hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance's hot wallets on October 29, about 4.2 times the 2025 Bybit hack.
Binance's SAFU reserve of about $1 billion to $1.2 billion equals roughly 16% to 19% of the loss.
Coinbase's disclosed $255 million crime policy would cover about 4% of a loss this size.
At 3% to 5% hot-wallet premiums, insuring $6.3 billion would cost about $189 million to $315 million a year.
Customers are being repaid from Binance's own funds, not insurance.
why_it_matters: Millions of people keep savings on crypto exchanges. The Binance hack shows that insurance covers only a small part of a major theft, so protection depends on the exchange's own finances.

title: Australian Home Cover Rises 6% as Rates Hit 4.85%: The Squeeze
summary: Australian home insurance prices are rising about 6% a year while motor cover is flat, on top of an RBA cash rate of 4.85% and inflation of 4.3%. Since 2010 home premiums have grown 7.2% a year against wages at 3.1%, which on our figures means premiums have risen 2.8 times while pay rose 1.6 times.
description:
Australian households are facing rising costs on two fronts. The Reserve Bank lifted its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its fifth increase this year and the highest level since 2008, after headline inflation reached 4.3% in the year to September. At the same time, home insurance premiums keep climbing. A Morgan Stanley survey found home insurance rates up about 6% year on year, while motor rates rose only about 1% as insurers competed for customers.

This PolicyRix Team analysis puts the long-run premium data alongside wages and inflation to show how far insurance has outrun incomes.

The long view

APRA's climate vulnerability assessment, published in March, found that home insurance premiums rose at an average of 7.2% a year between 2010 and 2025, while wages grew 3.1% a year. Compounded over 15 years, that means premiums rose about 2.8 times, while wages rose about 1.6 times. In other words, a policy that took one day's pay in 2010 would take close to two days' pay today, on our calculation.

Finity estimates the average premium rose from A$1,940 in 2020 to A$2,938 in the five years to October 2025, an increase of 51%, or about 8.7% a year compounded. Compare the Market found that home and contents quotes in the five largest capital cities rose an average of A$373.93, or 14.78%, in the 12 months to June 2026, about double the long-term pace. That implies an average quote of roughly A$2,900, up from about A$2,530.

Why premiums keep rising

Two forces dominate. The first is catastrophe losses. The Insurance Council of Australia says insurers handled 294,000 claims from declared extreme weather events in 2025, with the average cost per claim up 39% to A$16,471. On our arithmetic, that is about A$4.8 billion. The second is rebuilding costs: Cotality's construction index shows building costs rose about 30% in the five years to March 2026, against consumer price growth of about 24%. Home insurance pays to rebuild, so building costs feed directly into premiums.

Motor is different this year because insurers are cutting prices to win market share after several years of large increases. ASIC's August review of five motor insurers found none of their renewal notices adequately explained premiums that rose faster than inflation.

The household squeeze

The Actuaries Institute estimates 1.6 million households, about 15%, are in home insurance affordability stress, meaning premiums take more than four weeks of gross income. Some are cutting cover or going without. That creates a risk for lenders too, because a mortgage requires the home to be insured; APRA has warned that a growing share of homes could become uninsured over coming decades.

Higher interest rates make the squeeze worse. Mortgage repayments rise with each RBA increase, and insurance is one of the few large household bills that can feel optional. Dropping building cover is rarely sensible for a mortgaged home, but reviewing it is.

What households can do

Shop at renewal: quotes vary widely and loyalty is rarely rewarded. Check the sum insured against current rebuilding costs, which have risen faster than inflation, to avoid underinsurance. Consider a higher excess if you could afford it after a claim, which lowers the premium. Ask about discounts for resilience upgrades: several insurers now cut premiums for bushfire and cyclone-resilient features. And separate home and contents if one insurer is cheaper for each.

What the data cannot tell us

Averages hide big regional gaps: premiums in northern Queensland and flood-prone areas are many times the national average, while some city suburbs have seen small rises. Different data sources measure different things, quotes, renewals or averages across policies, so their figures do not match exactly. Our wage comparison uses average wage growth, not any individual's pay. And the 2025 loss figure depends on which events were declared catastrophes.

The short version: home insurance has risen far faster than pay for more than a decade, and with interest rates now climbing too, the squeeze on Australian homeowners is tightening.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of APRA, Finity, Compare the Market, Insurance Council of Australia, Actuaries Institute and RBA data, with reporting from Insurance Business
image_alt: Suburban house with a front garden (illustrative)
key_points: The RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its fifth hike this year, with inflation at 4.3%.
Home insurance rates are up about 6% a year while motor rates rose about 1%, per a Morgan Stanley survey.
APRA data shows premiums grew 7.2% a year from 2010 to 2025 against 3.1% wage growth: about 2.8 times versus 1.6 times on our calculation.
ICA figures imply about A$4.8 billion of 2025 extreme-weather claims, with average claim costs up 39%.
About 1.6 million households are in home insurance affordability stress, per the Actuaries Institute.
why_it_matters: Home insurance is a required cost for every mortgaged home. When premiums outpace pay and interest rates rise at the same time, more households cut cover, which leaves them and their lenders exposed.

title: Cowbell Launches Standalone Insurance for Damage Done by AI Agents
summary: Cowbell will sell a standalone policy from January 1, 2027 covering losses when AI agents used by small businesses make mistakes, move money wrongly or cause third-party claims. It arrives as 2,369 generative AI exclusion filings spread across 49 states.
description:
Cyber insurer Cowbell has announced what it calls the first standalone liability policy built for small and mid-sized businesses that let AI agents act on their behalf. Cowbell AI Liability Insurance will go on sale on January 1, 2027, through wholesale brokers on a non-admitted basis, which means it is written outside the standard state-approved forms.

What changed

AI agents are different from chatbots. They carry out tasks with little or no human approval: answering customers, issuing refunds, paying invoices, booking appointments or filing documents. When an agent makes a mistake, such as sending money to the wrong account or giving a customer wrong information, the loss can fall between existing policies.

Cowbell's policy uses a new trigger, an "AI incident," rather than the security breach that usually triggers cyber cover. According to the company, it covers first-party costs such as investigating and containing an incident, restoring operations, and financial losses from transactions an agent executes in error, as well as third-party claims from customers or others harmed by an agent's output. It also covers LLMjacking, where outsiders use stolen credentials or API keys to run up AI usage charges on a company's account. Cover is subject to limits, retentions and exclusions, and Cowbell has not published premiums.

Why it matters now

Standard policies are writing AI out. A review of state filings reported by Insurance Business found 2,369 generative AI exclusion records in force across 49 states by mid-2026, mostly in general liability forms, with no admitted standalone product to fill the gap. That leaves many businesses with less cover than they think as they adopt AI tools.

Cowbell says it will price the risk using three AI-specific factors that grade how an agent is monitored and constrained: for example, whether a human approves high-value actions, what systems and money the agent can reach, and how its activity is logged. Trent Cooksley, Cowbell's co-founder and chief operating officer, said small businesses are giving AI more responsibility for how they operate. Simon Hughes, chief commercial officer, said the product gives brokers a concrete solution for clients' agent risks.

What it means for small businesses

Any business using AI agents for customer service, payments or operations should check three things before renewal. First, read the general liability and cyber policies for AI exclusions, which may have been added at the last renewal. Second, ask whether a loss caused by an agent's mistake, with no hacker involved, would be covered anywhere. Third, look at controls: limits on what an agent can pay or approve, human sign-off for large transactions, and logs of what the agent did. Those controls reduce the chance of a loss and will likely affect the price of any AI cover.

Because the policy is non-admitted, it is not covered by state guaranty funds if the insurer fails, and its wording is not pre-approved by regulators. Businesses should ask a broker to compare the wording with any AI endorsements available from their existing insurers.

The wider market

Insurers have been cautious about AI because losses are new and hard to model. A handful of specialist products have appeared for large firms, often covering errors by AI models in specific uses. Cowbell's move into small businesses is notable because that is where AI agents are spreading fastest and where in-house risk management is thinnest. Expect more insurers to follow if early claims experience is manageable, and expect underwriters to ask more detailed questions about AI use at every renewal.
source_name: Cowbell announcement via PR Newswire; Insurance Business, SiliconANGLE and Insurtech Insights (November 10, 2026)
key_points: Cowbell AI Liability Insurance goes on sale January 1, 2027 through wholesale brokers on a non-admitted basis.
It is triggered by an 'AI incident', not a security breach, and covers first-party losses and third-party claims caused by AI agents.
Cover includes errors in transactions an agent executes and LLMjacking charges from stolen API keys.
2,369 generative AI exclusion filings were in force across 49 states by mid-2026.
Pricing uses three factors that grade how agents are monitored and constrained.
why_it_matters: Small businesses are adopting AI agents faster than their insurance is adapting, and many standard policies now exclude AI. Knowing where the gaps are helps owners avoid an uninsured loss.

title: IRDAI Starts Work on Risk-Based Capital Rules for Indian Insurers
summary: India's insurance regulator has set up two working groups, for life and non-life insurers, to design a risk-based capital regime built on Ind AS accounts. They have a month to produce draft rules, which would replace today's flat solvency formula with charges tied to each insurer's actual risks.
description:
India's insurance regulator has taken a concrete step toward one of the biggest changes in how insurers are supervised. In an order dated November 10, 2026, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) set up two working groups, one for life insurers and one for non-life insurers, to develop a risk-based capital (RBC) framework built on Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS).

What changed

Today, Indian insurers hold capital under a largely factor-based solvency regime: required capital is a set percentage of premiums, claims or reserves, with a minimum solvency ratio of 150%. That approach is simple but blunt. Two insurers with the same premium volume need similar capital even if one invests conservatively and writes stable business while the other takes far more risk.

Under RBC, capital charges would be calculated separately for market risk, underwriting risk, credit risk and operational risk, based on an economic balance sheet that values assets and liabilities realistically. Insurers that take more risk would need more capital; those that take less could hold less.

The working groups have been asked to prepare an exposure draft of RBC regulations for public consultation, an approach paper weighing different methods, and a regulatory reporting template. IRDAI wants the framework to use Ind AS financial statements as its starting point, so that insurers work from one set of data for accounts and solvency, with only transparent, justified prudential adjustments. The regulator said the result should be transparent, comparable across insurers, resistant to arbitrage, proportionate and achievable on a realistic timeline. The groups have a month to deliver.

How we got here

IRDAI approved Ind AS-based reporting for insurers from April 1, 2026, India's version of the IFRS 17 standard, with a one-year relief period and parallel reporting for up to two years. General insurers had asked for more time to implement both Ind AS and RBC. A parliamentary committee urged IRDAI in August to fast-track RBC to strengthen public sector insurers. Existing solvency rules remain in force until the new framework starts.

Why it matters for policyholders

Solvency rules exist to make sure insurers can pay claims in bad years. A risk-based system should do that more accurately: an insurer piling into risky investments or underpricing long-term guarantees would need to hold more capital, giving the regulator earlier warning. Over time, more accurate capital can also affect prices. Products that tie up a lot of capital, such as long-term savings plans with guaranteed returns, may become more expensive or less generous, while lower-risk products could become cheaper.

For investors in listed insurers, RBC could change reported solvency ratios, dividend capacity and the attractiveness of different product lines. Insurers with heavy guarantees or concentrated investments are most exposed.

What happens next

The working groups' drafts will go to public consultation, and insurers will then need time to build models, data systems and actuarial capacity. IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth has said India needs more qualified actuaries for the transition. Most global regimes of this kind, including Europe's Solvency II, took several years from design to full application, so a phased start with transition measures is likely.

What to watch

Key questions include how the life and non-life frameworks treat long-term guarantees, catastrophe risk and investments in government bonds; what the target capital level will be; and how long the transition period runs. The answers will shape product design and pricing in one of the world's fastest-growing insurance markets.
source_name: IRDAI order IRDAI/RBC/ORD/MISC/150/11/2026 via TaxGuru; Insurance Business, PSU Watch and Angel One
key_points: IRDAI set up life and non-life working groups on November 10, 2026 to design a risk-based capital framework.
The framework will build on Ind AS accounts, with capital charges for market, underwriting, credit and operational risk.
The groups must deliver draft regulations, an approach paper and a reporting template within a month.
Existing factor-based solvency rules, including the 150% minimum ratio, stay until RBC starts.
RBC could make capital-heavy products like guaranteed savings plans costlier over time.
why_it_matters: Capital rules decide how safely insurers can pay claims and which products they can afford to sell. Moving to risk-based capital will reshape Indian insurers' balance sheets, products and pricing.
